channel.title: HAT MI Daily - Macro and Industries
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Russia's federal budget deficit reached RUB 5.234 trillion, 2.3% of GDP, in the first ten months of 2026, above the RUB 3.786 trillion full-year plan, while oil and gas revenues fell 14.1%, according to preliminary Finance Ministry estimates.
item.description:
Interfax reports preliminary Finance Ministry estimates that Russia's federal budget deficit was RUB 5.234 trillion, or 2.3% of GDP, in the first ten months of 2026, against a full-year plan of RUB 3.786 trillion, or 1.6% of GDP. Revenues rose 11% year on year to RUB 33.176 trillion, of which RUB 26.734 trillion were non-oil and gas revenues (VAT revenue up 27.8% to RUB 14.701 trillion) and RUB 6.442 trillion were oil and gas revenues, down 14.1%. Expenditures rose 13.4% to RUB 38.41 trillion. The row does not name the comparison period for the oil and gas, VAT and expenditure changes, and does not say why VAT revenue rose, what drove the fall in oil and gas revenue, how the deficit is financed or whether the full-year plan will be revised.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports budget totals, not an output or trade measure. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a falling oil and gas revenue alongside a deficit above plan raises the state's dependence on other taxes and borrowing, which narrows its room for spending. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Russia matters through sanctions, energy and feedstock exports and their effect on European energy prices; the row gives no trade or chemical figures. Points that may be worth considering include Russia's oil and gas revenue for November and December, any revision of the 2026 budget plan and changes in sanctions or export quotas.

Interfax

item.title: US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October against 0.3% forecast, with core prices up 0.3%, and Fed governor Waller urged consideration of a 50-basis-point rise in December if core prices rose 0.3% or more, as two-year Treasury yields jumped.
item.description:
MarketScreener, citing a Reuters poll, reports that the US consumer price index rose 0.4% in October against 0.3% expected. The Chicago Tribune, citing the Labor Department, reports a 0.4% monthly rise after 0.6% in September, with core prices excluding food and energy up 0.3%, the same as in September; both figures were a tenth of a point above forecasts. MarketScreener adds, in a preview of the release, that the Bureau of Labor Statistics would not publish year-on-year readings because the 2025 government shutdown prevented price collection in October 2025. The Standard reports that Fed governor Christopher Waller would support a 25-basis-point rise in December and said a 50-basis-point rise should be considered if core prices rose 0.3% or more; The Financial Times reports that he urged policymakers to consider 50 basis points in December if the data do not soon show a rapid cooling of inflation. Anadolu Agency reports Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan calling for at least two more quarter-point rises, potentially at a faster pace this winter, and suggesting a pause afterward to assess whether further tightening is necessary; Bloomberg reports JPMorgan Asset Management's David Kelly saying a half-point rise is not needed next month. Business Recorder reports the CME FedWatch tool pricing almost a 99% chance of a December rise. Bloomberg reports two-year Treasury yields up 17 basis points to 4.73%, the biggest jump since April 2025, while Business Recorder puts the rise at 21.4 basis points. The rows do not give the level of the Fed's policy rate or the components of the October rise.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a monthly price rise and officials' remarks about possible rate moves, not a decision. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, higher expected US interest rates raise borrowing costs for housing, construction and capital-goods buyers and tend to strengthen the dollar, which affects the cost of imported inputs outside the US. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, US housing starts, construction spending and vehicle and equipment sales are demand drivers, and higher mortgage and financing costs would weigh on them with a delay; the rows give no sector data. Points that may be worth considering include the November consumer price index, the Fed's December decision and US mortgage rates.

MarketScreener | MarketScreener | Chicago Tribune | The Standard | The Financial Times | Anadolu Agency | Bloomberg | Business Recorder | Bloomberg

item.title: Profits of Chinese industrial enterprises above designated size rose 15.5% on year in the first three quarters of 2026, with electronics profits doubling, non-metallic minerals down 46.9% and car-making down 22.8%, China Daily reports.
item.description:
China Daily reports that profits of industrial enterprises above the designated size in China rose 15.5% year on year in the first three quarters of 2026. Profits in computers, communication and other electronic equipment doubled, while profits in non-metallic mineral products fell 46.9% and in automotive manufacturing fell 22.8%. High-tech manufacturing value added rose 14.3% in the first nine months, 9 percentage points faster than overall industrial value added, and output of 3D printing equipment, lithium-ion batteries and industrial robots rose 62.5%, 39.5% and 29.1% respectively. The row does not say which agency published the data or when, what the designated size means in revenue terms, the profit levels in yuan or which products the non-metallic mineral group contains.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports profits, value added and output growth for a few high-tech products, not production volumes or prices for construction materials or vehicles. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, non-metallic mineral products include construction materials such as cement, glass and ceramics, so a 46.9% fall in their profits is consistent with weak construction demand or price pressure, and a 22.8% fall in car-making profits is consistent with a weak domestic car market, while electronics and batteries are growing. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, construction materials, vehicles, electronics and batteries are all customer industries, so the split between falling and rising profits indicates where demand for bonding and sealing materials in China may be moving; the row gives no volumes. Points that may be worth considering include China's full-year industrial profit data and output of construction materials.

China Daily

item.title: France blames Shahid Kaveh, a hacking unit reportedly linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guard, for an October cyberattack on refrigeration at about 700 retail sites causing tens of millions of euros in food losses, and plans to propose EU sanctions.
item.description:
Axios reports that France's Cyber Crisis Coordination Center blames Shahid Kaveh, a hacking unit within Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (Dünya Gazetesi says only that it is reportedly linked to the Guard), for cyberattacks that disrupted refrigeration systems at roughly 700 grocery stores and other retail locations in October, causing tens of millions of euros in food losses and at least 15 fires; the same operation also targeted equipment at small hydroelectric facilities in France with limited effects, according to an intelligence report. Dünya Gazetesi reports that the attacks took place on the night of 11-12 October, that, according to the investigation, the attackers remotely accessed the web interfaces of cooling control units, disabled the high-temperature warnings and started a continuous defrost cycle, and that Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said those held responsible could face entry bans and asset freezes, while the Foreign Ministry announced that new European sanctions would be proposed. The Nation reports that Barrot called it the first large-scale cyberattack for sabotage purposes on French territory and that Iran rejected the accusation as baseless and hostile. The rows give no sanctions list or timetable. Dünya Gazetesi adds that investigators reportedly detected the use of Farsi and IP addresses pointing to devices in Iran and that a Paris prosecutor has applied for an international arrest warrant, but the rows give no further evidence, and Iran's denial appears in one row only.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a government attribution and an announced intention to propose sanctions, not adopted measures. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, the kind of attack France describes, manipulating refrigeration equipment remotely through web interfaces, points to the risk that building and industrial control systems can be sabotaged remotely, and new sanctions on Iranian individuals and organisations would be an additional measure. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, production plants may use comparable control systems and food-retail and cold-chain customers use packaging and labelling materials, so an attack on either could disrupt operations or demand; the rows give no figures for either. Points that may be worth considering include the content and timing of any EU sanctions list and further attacks attributed to the same group on European industrial sites.

Axios | The Financial Times | Dünya Gazetesi | The Nation

item.title: Chancellor Merz, in a letter to Commission President von der Leyen, publicly backs the EU's emissions trading course for the first time and seeks investment security, while chemical and steel companies warn of competitive losses, Handelsblatt reports.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that Chancellor Friedrich Merz has for the first time publicly supported the EU's course on emissions trading (ETS) in a letter to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, calling for the EU to ensure investment security in the system; the row adds that the market-based system should be maintained. According to Handelsblatt, the Commission plans to extend the auctioning of certificates and give companies more time for climate protection under the reform, while companies in the chemical and steel industries warn of competitive losses and demand changes. Handelsblatt says EU member states and the European Parliament are to agree a common position on the reform by the end of the year. Les Echos reports that the Commission proposed the reform in July, that the system is accused of harming the competitiveness of European industry, and that the Commission wants a compromise quickly, if possible before the next French presidential elections, which requires the Parliament and the Council to develop their versions by the end of the year before a trilogue agreement in a few months. The two rows describe the year-end step differently (a common position of member states and Parliament in Handelsblatt, separate Parliament and Council versions before a trilogue agreement in Les Echos). The rows do not give the text of Merz's letter beyond these points, the auction volumes or timetable proposed, the changes the chemical and steel companies demand or the date of any vote.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a government position and an ongoing legislative process, not a decision on the reform. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, the carbon price and the rules on free allocation and auctioning of certificates determine energy and process costs for energy-intensive producers, so a compromise that keeps the system largely as proposed, or one that eases it, would change cost expectations for the chemical industry. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the effect would reach through the energy and feedstock costs of resin, solvent and additive suppliers, passed on with a lag; the rows give no cost figures. Points that may be worth considering include the Parliament's and the Council's positions at year-end, any change to the proposed auctioning schedule and statements from chemical industry associations.

Handelsblatt | Les Echos

item.title: Chinese carmakers seeking European production sites have so far avoided Germany, which supplier network AMZ calls too expensive for volume production, while Spain and Hungary offer better funding and lower taxes.
item.description:
Süddeutsche Zeitung reports that Chinese carmakers are increasingly focusing on production in Europe, but that Germany and Saxony have not yet benefited, according to industry experts. Süddeutsche Zeitung and Wallstreet:online say Volkswagen is reducing capacity in Saxony and not only there, while Chinese manufacturers look for new European sites and have so far avoided Saxony and Germany as a whole despite its long automotive tradition. An analysis by the automotive supplier network AMZ for the Automotive Forum in Zwickau finds that Germany is too expensive for volume production and that other EU countries, such as Spain and Hungary, offer more attractive funding conditions and a lower tax burden. The rows do not give the number or capacity of planned Chinese plants, the sites chosen, the funding amounts or tax rates compared, or which Chinese carmakers are meant.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report an industry network's analysis and expert views, not announced investment decisions. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, where new vehicle plants are built decides where their suppliers locate and where materials are bought, so plants in Spain or Hungary instead of Germany would shift that demand. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle assembly and battery plants are large users of bonding, sealing and coating materials, and new plants outside Germany would draw on suppliers and qualification work in those countries; the rows give no volumes. Points that may be worth considering include announcements of specific Chinese plants in Europe, the state aid granted for them and the pace of capacity cuts at German plants.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | Wallstreet:online

item.title: China's Ministry of Commerce extended its pause on rare earth export controls by two months, to January, covering several rare earths and related technologies, lithium batteries and synthetic graphite anode material, the South China Morning Post reports.
item.description:
The South China Morning Post reports that the Ministry of Commerce in Beijing announced a two-month extension of its rare earth export control pause, to January. The pause covers several rare earths and related technologies, as well as lithium batteries and synthetic graphite anode material. Bernd Schaefer, chief executive of EIT RawMaterials, a European Union co-funded group of companies, universities and research institutes in the raw materials sector, said the extension highlighted the need for Europe to diversify its rare earth supply to ensure predictable and continued access. European industry insiders welcomed a positive change of mindset in the bloc's efforts to reduce its dependency on imports of rare earths and other raw materials but cautioned that problems remain, especially in financing and regulations, and analysts warned the EU was running out of time. The row does not give the date of the announcement, the exact date in January on which the pause ends, which products and technologies are covered beyond those named, the volumes at stake or any reaction from the United States, and it is the only row in the input on this extension.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a Chinese decision to prolong an existing pause, not new restrictions or a settlement. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a pause that is extended in short steps keeps supply of the covered materials open while leaving the option of reinstating controls, which makes planning and stock-holding harder for users. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, rare earths are used in magnets, electronics and some catalysts, and lithium batteries and graphite anode material feed electric vehicle and electronics supply chains whose assembly uses bonding, sealing and thermal-management materials; the row gives no volumes or prices. Points that may be worth considering include the date on which the pause ends, any widening of the product list and the EU's measures on raw material supply.

South China Morning Post

item.title: German real estate prices rose 0.2% in the third quarter from a year earlier and fell 0.2% from the second quarter, the vdp index shows, with residential prices up 1.0% on the year and office prices down 3.9%.
item.description:
Wallstreet:online reports that the real estate price index of the Association of German Pfandbrief Banks (vdp) shows prices in Germany remained stable in the third quarter: up 0.2% on the same quarter a year earlier and down 0.2% on the previous quarter. Residential property prices rose 1.0% year on year and moved sideways on the quarter (down 0.1%). Retail property prices were unchanged on the year (0.0%) and up 0.1% on the quarter. Office property prices fell 3.9% year on year and 1.0% on the quarter. The row does not give price levels, the regional split, the weight of each property type in the index, transaction volumes or any construction activity figure.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports prices, which are a different measure from construction output or demand for building materials. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, stable residential prices alongside falling office prices point to a market where homes hold their value while office space loses it, and price levels influence whether new building and renovation projects are started. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, construction and renovation are large end-markets, and refurbishment of existing buildings uses bonding, sealing and coating materials as well as new building; the row gives no volumes. Points that may be worth considering include German building permits and construction output for September and October and the next vdp index release.

Wallstreet:online

item.title: The average accounts-payable and notes-payable turnover period of 14 Chinese carmakers rose to 187.5 days in the first half of 2026 from 164.4 at end-2025, The Diplomat reports, and Bloomberg counts USD 269 billion of value lost since September 2025.
item.description:
The Diplomat reports that the average accounts-payable and notes-payable turnover period of 14 automakers in China reached 187.5 days in the first half of 2026, compared with 164.4 days at the end of 2025. It adds that the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers stated an average payment period of 54 days, about 10 days shorter than a year earlier. The two figures are labelled differently (turnover period and payment period) and move in opposite directions; the row does not say how either is calculated, whether they cover the same companies or which 14 companies are included. Bloomberg reports that Chinese automakers have lost USD 269 billion in value, a 45% fall, since peaking at nearly USD 600 billion in September 2025, as competition squeezes profits; Xiaomi accounts for nearly USD 95 billion of the loss and BYD, whose shares fell 38%, for USD 37 billion, and every Chinese carmaker tracked is well below its peak. The rows do not say what the market value covers or give profit figures, supplier names or payment terms by supplier.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a turnover period and market values, not payments made to suppliers or order volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a longer payables turnover period means suppliers wait longer for payment, which ties up their working capital and raises their exposure to the customer, while competition that squeezes margins can lead carmakers to press suppliers on price. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, bonding, sealing and coating materials are bought by carmakers and their tier-one suppliers, so payment terms and price pressure in China may affect the margins and credit exposure of suppliers serving them; the rows give no figures for materials suppliers. Points that may be worth considering include the full-year payables figures, the association's payment-period data and further changes in carmakers' market value.

The Diplomat | Bloomberg

item.title: Ardagh Group is considering shutting one glass melting furnace each at Holmegaard in Denmark and Knottingley in Britain, after capacity adjustments in Germany, against weak demand for glass packaging, particularly in Northern Europe.
item.description:
BVSE (Bundesverband Sekundärrohstoffe und Entsorgung) reports that Ardagh Group is considering the shutdown of two further glass melting furnaces, one at the Holmegaard site in Denmark and one at the Knottingley site in Great Britain, following capacity adjustments already made in Germany. The row says the proposals are being discussed with local company managements and employee representatives, although one sentence of the row says the furnaces "are to be shut down", so the row is not consistent on whether a decision has been taken. It gives the background as weak demand for glass packaging, particularly in Northern Europe, which remains significantly below historical levels and has led to excess production capacity, and as persistently high energy prices and inflation-related cost increases weighing on the profitability of glass production. The row does not give the furnaces' capacity, the number of jobs affected, a timetable, the scale of the German adjustments or demand figures, and it is the only row on the subject.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a proposal at one company, with sector-level demand and cost statements given as background. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, glass containers compete with metal, plastic and carton packaging, and furnace closures in a market with excess capacity cut supply while also signalling weak demand from beverage and food filling. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, glass packaging uses labels, closures and secondary packaging that rely on adhesives and coatings, so lower glass container output could reduce demand for those materials in the affected regions, while a shift of filling to other packaging formats would move that demand; the row gives no figures for either. Points that may be worth considering include the outcome of the talks with employee representatives, further closure announcements from other glass producers and European glass container demand data.

BVSE
